Volatility has stayed low throughout - USD/CHF 3M implied at 6.67% and EUR/CHF at 3.77% - which is itself the mechanism: cheap volatility plus a wide rate gap is what makes a funding trade scalable.

tactical.analysis: The SNB policy rate is 0.00%, the lowest of all eleven benchmark currencies and 100bp below the next-lowest (BoJ at 1.00%), which places the franc dead last at 11/11 on the single most heavily weighted factor in the framework. The policy spread runs from -100bp versus JPY through -175bp versus SEK, -225bp versus EUR and CAD, -250bp versus NZD, -363bp versus USD, -375bp versus GBP, -425bp versus NOK to -435bp versus AUD; there is not one peer against which the franc earns positive carry. The term structure repeats the story: the Swiss 10Y Confederation yield is 0.475% against 4.67% for the US 10Y (-419.5bp), 3.18% for the Bund (-270.5bp) and 2.801% for the JGB (-232.6bp), and the 2Y gap to the US is -408bp. Crucially the gaps are widening rather than closing: the US 10Y rose from 4.44% at end-June to 4.67% at 2026-07-29 while Swiss yields were anchored by a central bank that has publicly assumed zero for three years. On the front end, SARON fixed at -0.04% on 2026-07-30, i.e. Swiss overnight money is already negative in practice even with the policy rate at zero, and the SNB's lowering of the sight-deposit threshold factor from 15 to 13.5 effective 2026-08-01 mechanically increases the volume of bank reserves remunerated at policy minus 25bp. The SNB itself states the threshold change has no impact on the monetary policy stance, and that is technically correct, but at the margin it makes holding franc cash fractionally more costly for Swiss banks in the exact fortnight the tactical horizon covers. Meanwhile the Fed is priced to hike on 2026-09-16 after three hawkish dissents on 2026-07-29, the ECB is priced to hike on 2026-09-10, the BoJ carries an 81% cumulative hike probability by December, the BoE is 65% priced for September and the RBNZ has already gone. The 2s10s Swiss curve at roughly +33.5bp is mildly positive but the entire Swiss curve sits below the lowest point of every peer curve, so there is no part of the franc term structure that offers a tactical yield refuge.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the franc's rate disadvantage is not merely persistent, it is scheduled to deepen. The SNB's June conditional inflation forecast of 0.6% for 2026, 0.6% for 2027 and 0.7% for 2028 is explicitly constructed on the assumption that the policy rate remains at 0% across the entire horizon, and the forecast sits comfortably inside the 0-2% price-stability band at every point, which removes any internally consistent reason for the SNB to move. Against that, Norges Bank has published a path 'just above 4.5 percent at the end of the year', the RBNZ is expected to reach roughly 3.00% by December, the Fed's June dot plot centres on 3.6-4.1% for end-2026, the ECB has around three 25bp hikes priced over the coming year and the BoJ is expected at 1.25%. Simple arithmetic on those paths widens the average CHF policy disadvantage from roughly 269bp today to roughly 295-305bp by January 2027. The forward market has already monetised part of this: USD/CHF 6M forward points are -166.58, an outright of 0.79113 and a 4.12% annualised franc appreciation cushion, which means a long-franc position must beat a 4% annualised hurdle just to break even. The strategic bear case is not that the SNB will ease further - a return to negative rates is possible but Chairman Schlegel has repeatedly set a high bar and stated a preference for FX intervention - it is that the SNB has removed itself as a variable entirely, leaving the franc's rate profile to be determined by what every other central bank does. The one genuine two-way risk is that the energy shock proves persistent: Brent at 91.82 versus 70.46 at end-June (level flagged - see Factor 5) has already lifted Swiss headline inflation from 0.1% in February to 0.5% in June, and a sustained move above 1% would force a repricing of the 2027 path. Confidence is a notch below tactical precisely because six months contains two SNB assessments (2026-09-24 and 2026-12-10) and a full December Monetary Policy Report.

The offsetting forces are therefore real and roughly balanced in magnitude: a scheduled, dated, quantified growth hit against an energy-driven inflation impulse of uncertain persistence. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months positioning remains a non-signal, but the composition of the flows matters more than the level. The structural story is that the franc has been reassigned as the world's preferred funding currency: ING wrote on 2026-07-28 that a Bloomberg-sourced report of SNB insiders seeing zero rates until end-2027 'will also point carry trade investors to increasingly fund out of Swiss francs rather than the yen', because franc funding is cheaper and avoids the risk of Bank of Japan intervention 'to the tune of $70bn, which could trigger a quick 3-4% drawdown for yen-funded carry trades'. That kind of flow does not show up in CME futures; it shows up in cross-border bank lending and in the FX swap market, neither of which is visible in the free data. The implication for the strategic horizon is that the true short-franc position is materially larger than the USD 7.19bn visible on the CME, and that it is held by participants with longer holding periods and less sensitivity to weekly volatility than macro hedge funds. That cuts both ways: it means the position is stickier and less prone to a fast squeeze, but it also means that if it does unwind - which requires a volatility shock rather than a valuation trigger - the move would be far larger than the futures data implies. The official-sector side is the other strategic consideration. SNB sight deposits rising 2.2% over three months and foreign currency investments at CHF 786.06bn tell us the SNB remains an active, if modest, seller of francs. The SNB's constraint has also loosened: the US Treasury retained Switzerland on its currency monitoring list but Switzerland now meets only one of the three criteria - the current-account surplus, cited at 7.0% of GDP or roughly USD 73bn - and would be removed at the next report if it meets fewer than two. A less constrained SNB is a franc-negative development at the margin.

factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning is not stretched and there is no contrarian trade available. For the franc, given open interest of roughly 108,000 contracts, 'stretched' begins around a combined speculative net beyond plus or minus 30,000 to 35,000 contracts in either direction, and at -46,455 combined the position is past that marker in absolute terms but sits at only the 52nd blended percentile of the cached window because the historical distribution is itself skewed short. The unwind trigger would have to be exogenous: a VIX close above 26 for three sessions, a Fed pivot at the 2026-09-16 FOMC, or a Middle East escalation lifting Brent above 115. A squeeze on futures alone would be small - covering the entire leveraged-fund short of 8,897 contracts is USD 1.38bn, roughly a normal London morning in USD/CHF - so the violence would come not from the CME but from the unmeasured funding book, where a 3-4% move in a fortnight is the historical template for a funding-currency unwind. The contrarian case is that the shorts already covered in July without a rally, which is precisely the evidence that this is not a positioning-driven market.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: Strategically the contrarian question is sharper: what does the other side of the trade see? A franc bull buys the third-largest current-account surplus in the benchmark set at 9.77% of GDP, an AAA sovereign with 37.6% debt-to-GDP, a net international investment position of CHF 974bn, and a real effective exchange rate at only the 40th percentile - a structurally scarce asset trading at a fair rather than a rich price, financed at effectively zero. That is a genuinely coherent thesis and it is why the strategic weighted score is only -0.240 rather than -0.5. The squeeze severity question is answered by history: the closest analogue is January 2015, when the removal of the EUR/CHF floor produced an intraday move of roughly 30%. Nothing of that scale is in prospect, but the episode establishes that franc positioning unwinds are discontinuous rather than orderly, and that low realised volatility beforehand is not protective. Our resolution is that the strategic contrarian case is real but requires a catalyst we cannot date, so it belongs in the invalidator list and the tail-hedge discussion rather than in the central stance.

tactical.analysis: At the two-to-four-week horizon the external balance is a background constant rather than a driver, and the signals within it currently offset. Switzerland's current-account surplus is 9.77% of GDP on the OECD-harmonised measure for Q1 2026, behind Singapore's 17.50% and Norway's 15.59% in the benchmark set and far above the United States at -2.85%, the United Kingdom at -2.84% and Australia at -3.68%. That surplus is the structural reason the franc appreciates in real terms over decades, but it does not transmit to spot inside a month. What can transmit inside a month is the commodity channel, and there the reading is franc-negative: Switzerland imports energy and raw materials and exports high-value manufactured goods, so Brent at 91.82 - up 30.3% from 70.46 at end-June and 25.0% above its year-ago level - is a terms-of-trade deterioration, and the SNB itself attributed the rise in Swiss inflation from 0.1% to 0.6% principally to oil products. The second commodity channel is gold, where the linkage is a shared safe-haven demand function rather than a trade relationship: XAU/USD at 4,054.45 is down 12.14% over three months and 17.94% over six, and the framework's direction rule that rising gold supports the franc has been running in reverse all year. Set against that, the SNB's Q1 2026 balance-of-payments release showed a current-account surplus of CHF 16bn, down CHF 11bn on Q1 2025 with the deterioration mainly in goods including a non-monetary gold deficit - a reminder that Swiss monthly and quarterly trade data is distorted by the country's role as the world's largest gold refining hub and must be read with that adjustment. The Q2 trade data was firmer: a CHF 13.9bn surplus with exports of CHF 73.2bn, up 8.8% quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted, though real export growth was only 0.6%. Level strong, momentum negative, no tactical signal.

tactical.what_is_priced: Nothing in the current spot rate reflects the external balance - a currency backed by a near-10%-of-GDP surplus does not normally trade at the 22nd percentile of its own twelve-month strength range. strategic.analysis: At the strategic horizon, where this factor carries a 0.16 weight - the second heaviest in the framework - the external balance is the strongest single franc-positive fact in the dossier and it is the reason the strategic weighted score is only -0.240 rather than approaching -0.5. Switzerland runs a current-account surplus of 9.77% of GDP, has done so persistently for decades, and holds a net international investment position of CHF 974bn as of Q1 2026. The surplus is structurally diversified across a goods surplus in pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and watches, a services surplus in financial services and commodity trading, and a large primary income surplus on overseas investments - three independent legs, which is why it has survived every shock of the last twenty years. That flow creates persistent, price-insensitive demand for francs which reasserts itself whenever the cyclical funding-outflow story pauses. The honest counterweight is that the surplus is deteriorating at the margin and faces a dated, quantified threat: the Q1 surplus fell CHF 11bn year-on-year, and Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs at a 15% capped rate took effect on 2026-07-31 for the seventeen largest importers and extend to all others on 2026-09-29, striking directly at the largest component. Switzerland negotiated that cap down from a 39% headline rate and from a Section 232 structure that reaches 100% for other jurisdictions, in exchange for a USD 200bn Swiss corporate investment pledge in the United States by 2028 - which is itself a multi-year franc-selling capital outflow. Netting it: a 15% tariff on the pharma line and a phased USD 200bn outflow will compress the surplus by perhaps 1-2 percentage points of GDP over several years, taking it from roughly 10% to roughly 8% - still third in the set behind Singapore and Norway, and still overwhelmingly supportive. Level dominates change over one to six months.

tactical.analysis: The SNB's communication is unusually explicit and unusually franc-negative. At the 2026-06-18 monetary policy assessment the Governing Board left the policy rate at 0.00% and stated: 'If necessary, the SNB has an increased willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market. The SNB thereby counters a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc.' That is a one-directional reaction function stated in plain language - the SNB has committed to lean against franc strength and has said nothing about leaning against franc weakness. It reinforced the point in its risk section: 'The upward pressure on the Swiss franc could also increase again.' The conditional inflation forecast is the second and more consequential signal. At 0.6% for 2026, 0.6% for 2027 and 0.7% for 2028, it sits inside the 0-2% band at every point on the horizon and, critically, 'is based on the assumption that the SNB policy rate is 0% over the entire forecast horizon'. A central bank that publishes a three-year forecast conditioned on zero and then declares that forecast satisfactory has effectively pre-committed to zero. Chairman Schlegel has separately and repeatedly set a high bar for negative rates on the grounds of 'undesirable side effects' including real-estate price pressure, and has indicated a preference for FX intervention over sub-zero policy, while also stating that the SNB has no exchange-rate target. Credibility is high: the SNB has done what it said at every assessment since the June 2025 cut, and a Reuters poll of 29 forecasters found 28 expecting no change through 2026. The structural caveat is that the SNB is a three-person Governing Board meeting four times a year with minimal forward guidance, and January 2015 remains the market's reference point for how discontinuous SNB surprises can be. Tactically, however, there is no scheduled SNB communication event before 2026-09-24, which means the current guidance stands unchallenged through the entire two-to-four-week window.

strategic.analysis: Guidance carries a 0.12 strategic weight, nearly double its tactical weight, and over one to six months the SNB's communication becomes the binding constraint on the franc rather than mere context. The core point is that the SNB has removed itself as a source of positive surprise. Its conditional forecast conditions on zero through 2028; Bloomberg-sourced reporting that SNB insiders see the policy rate at 0.00% until end-2027 has been circulating since late July and was the specific trigger ING cited on 2026-07-28 for carry investors rotating their funding leg from yen into francs; Commerzbank published on 2026-07-29 that SNB rates are seen on prolonged hold to end-2027 and that reports of a hold into early 2028 'clash with still-ambitious market expectations for hikes by 2027'. When a central bank's guidance is this clear and this durable, the currency loses its optionality, and a currency without policy optionality that also has the lowest yield in its peer group is definitionally a funding currency. The intervention pledge compounds this asymmetrically: 'increased willingness to intervene' means the SNB will sell francs into strength but has given no indication it would buy francs into weakness, and the constraint that historically moderated that behaviour has just loosened - the US Treasury retained Switzerland on its monitoring list but Switzerland now meets only one of three criteria and would be removed at the next report if it meets fewer than two. A less constrained SNB with a one-sided reaction function is a structurally capped currency. The two-way risk is the SNB's own history: the abandonment of the EUR/CHF floor in January 2015 was completely un-telegraphed, and a three-person board meeting four times a year with minimal guidance retains a genuine capacity to surprise, in either direction. That is why confidence is 68 rather than higher, and why the strategic risk-reward section carries an explicit discontinuity warning.

tactical.analysis: The event calendar for the franc is genuinely two-sided over the next four weeks, which is why this is a reasoned Neutral. The dated, known, franc-negative event has just landed: Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs took effect on 2026-07-31 at a 15% capped rate for Switzerland, applying immediately to the seventeen companies named in Annex III of the April 2026 proclamation, with all other importers captured from 2026-09-29. Pharmaceuticals are Switzerland's largest export category to the United States, and Commerzbank explicitly attributed short-term franc pressure on 2026-07-28 to the combination of fresh US tariffs and weak Swiss exports. Against that, the undated franc-positive tail is the Middle East, and its magnitude is not hypothetical: Brent traded from 70.46 at end-June to 91.82 on 2026-07-27, having reached 126.69 in March 2026 on Strait of Hormuz disruption, and the SNB's own June assessment named the Middle East as the primary source of forecast uncertainty. The domestic Swiss political calendar is close to irrelevant - federal popular votes fall on 2026-09-27 and 2026-11-29, both outside the tactical window and neither carrying FX consequence, and Swiss political risk is structurally the lowest in the developed world. The Swiss-EU Bilaterals III package was signed in March 2026 and is in ratification, but the referendum is not expected before 2027 and possibly 2028 to avoid disrupting the 2027 federal elections, so it is a background rather than a live risk. Options markets are pricing the event landscape roughly correctly with a modest front-end premium: USD/CHF one-week implied vol at 7.65% sits 1.13 points above the one-month at 6.52%, a visible but not extreme kink around early-August Swiss CPI, US data and the tariff onset. Netting a dated, quantified, already-negotiated negative against an undated but potentially large positive gives no directional edge.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the event landscape stays balanced but the individual items get larger. The dated franc-negatives are the full extension of pharmaceutical tariffs to all importers on 2026-09-29 and the cumulative drag of the USD 200bn Swiss corporate investment pledge into the United States, which is by construction a multi-year franc-selling capital outflow. The dated franc-neutral-to-positive item is the 2026-09-24 SNB assessment, the single largest scheduled Swiss event in the window, where the risk is two-sided: a downgraded inflation forecast revives the negative-rate conversation and is franc-negative, while an upgraded forecast on persistent energy pass-through would validate the market's hawkish premium and is franc-positive. The undated risks dominate the distribution. A Middle East re-escalation is the fastest and largest available franc-positive and the March 2026 episode demonstrated the transmission works. Swiss banking-sector concentration is a genuine structural tail: UBS is now the dominant Swiss bank following the 2023 Credit Suisse absorption, and any UBS-specific stress would be systemic for the franc, though nothing in current data suggests it is live. The neutrality question is worth stating precisely: Switzerland's adoption of EU sanctions against Russia tested the traditional neutrality stance, and any further erosion of that perception would degrade the haven premium structurally - a slow, low-probability, high-impact channel. Swiss-EU ratification noise builds through the window without resolving. Netting a scheduled negative of known and capped magnitude against an unscheduled positive of unknown but potentially large magnitude produces no directional signal, and forcing one would introduce noise into a weighted score where this factor carries only 0.05.

tactical.analysis: Swiss fiscal and sovereign risk is not currently material and will not move the franc inside four weeks; the high confidence attached to this Neutral reflects certainty about the absence of a signal, not indecision. Switzerland is rated AAA by every major agency, with Morningstar DBRS most recently confirming the Swiss Confederation at AAA with a Stable trend on 2025-07-18. FLAGGED: that confirmation is 379 days old, well outside the 60-day strategic freshness window, and no 2026 Swiss rating action exists - the rating is presented as best available rather than as current, and general government debt at 37.6% of GDP is among the lowest of all AAA sovereigns. The federal debt brake, in force since 2003, mandates a balanced budget over the business cycle and has kept Switzerland structurally near balance for two decades. There is no bond supply problem: the Confederation issues sparingly, the 10Y yields 0.475%, and Swiss sovereign CDS is effectively unquoted because there is no meaningful demand to hedge the credit. None of the conditions under which this factor becomes dominant are present - there is no emerging debt crisis, no announced fiscal regime change, no rating agency action or watch listing, no debt ceiling dynamic and no bond market stress. The single analytically useful observation is comparative rather than absolute: the franc's fiscal backdrop is a relative differentiator in a set where the UK 10Y yields 5.04% against a -2.84% current account, the US runs a -2.85% external balance with a 4.67% ten-year, and euro-area sovereign issuance is expanding. That relative quality is real, but it is also fully embedded in a 0.475% ten-year yield - the market has already paid for it in full, which is precisely why it generates no tactical signal. There is no new information in this factor and no scheduled event inside the tactical window that could create any.

strategic.analysis: At the strategic horizon Swiss fiscal strength converts from an inert fact into a modest directional support, which is why the stance shifts from Neutral to Bullish while the confidence falls to 55 to reflect how slow and how already-priced the channel is. The mechanism is relative, not absolute. Switzerland's 37.6% debt-to-GDP and constitutionally entrenched debt brake are static; what is changing is the peer group. The UK ten-year at 5.04% is the highest in the benchmark set and embeds a fiscal risk premium rather than pure carry; the United States runs a -2.85% current account alongside a 4.67% ten-year and an expanding issuance programme; euro-area sovereign supply is rising with defence and energy commitments, with the Bund at 3.18% up sharply from the levels of a year ago. In that environment the scarcity value of a genuinely unimpeachable sovereign balance sheet increases, and it is the substrate on which the franc's haven function rests - capital flight to Switzerland is ultimately a flight to a sovereign credit, not to a yield. This channel also interacts directly with Factor 5: the current-account surplus is recycled abroad rather than absorbed domestically precisely because the Confederation does not need to issue, which is why Switzerland has a CHF 974bn net international investment position. Over one to six months the practical expression of this is a floor rather than a driver: it is the reason our downside scenario for the franc stops at USD/CHF 0.8600 rather than extending, and the reason a franc that is cheap on carry does not become cheap on credit. Confidence is held at 55 because there is no plausible catalyst inside the window - no Swiss rating action is pending and no peer downgrade is scheduled - so this is a background support with an uncertain trigger date.

Volatility regime points the same way: at EUR/CHF three-month implied of 3.77% the franc funding trade is scalable at high leverage, and low-volatility trends persist until something breaks them. But the option skew points the other way and does so with increasing force as tenor extends - EUR/CHF 25-delta risk reversals run -0.29 at one month, -0.47 at three, -0.59 at six and -0.74 at one year, a monotonically increasing premium for franc calls. The vol term structure in contango out to 7.18% at one year says the market expects volatility to rise from here even without a dated catalyst. Key structural levels frame the strategic range: on the downside for the franc, the 52-week USD/CHF high at 0.81938 is the immediate objective, above which there is little historical reference until the 0.83-0.85 zone and ING's stated 0.85 August target; on the upside for the franc, the 200-day at 0.7927 is the regime line and the 52-week low at 0.76602 is the full haven re-engagement level. On EUR/CHF, parity at 1.0000 remains the defining psychological level as the former SNB floor, but at 0.9317 it sits 7.3% above spot and is not reachable inside the strategic window under any scenario we assign meaningful probability to - the practical strategic ceiling is UBS's 0.9500. The honest summary is a franc-negative trend structure carrying a well-bid franc-positive tail.

factors.expression_assessment: The volatility landscape argues for expressing a bearish franc view in spot or forwards rather than options, and for buying the tail hedge separately rather than embedding it. Three observations drive that. First, twenty-day realised volatility on USD/CHF at 6.9% exceeds one-month implied at 6.52%, so the market is delivering more movement than it charges for - directional spot exposure is being rewarded relative to premium-paying structures. Second, the skew is against the view: risk reversals are negative from three months outward on USD/CHF and at every tenor on EUR/CHF, meaning franc calls carry a rising premium, so any structure that finances a bearish-franc position by selling franc calls is selling the cheap side and any structure that buys franc puts pays the expensive side. Third, the forward curve already pays the entire carry - a 6M USD/CHF outright of 0.79113 against spot 0.80779 delivers 166.58 points before any spot move - so a forward expression monetises the rate differential without paying time value. Separately, because EUR/CHF three-month implied volatility of 3.77% is exceptionally low in absolute terms, a small outright EUR/CHF put position is the cheapest available protection against the one scenario that breaks the thesis, and the front-end vol kink (1W 7.65% versus 1M 6.52%) argues for establishing exposure after the early-August Swiss CPI and US data cluster rather than into it.

tactical.analysis: Global dollar funding conditions are benign and abundant, and for the franc that is unambiguously negative because ample USD liquidity is the precondition for the carry trades that are funded in francs. SOFR fixed at 3.65% on 2026-07-30 against a fed funds effective rate of 3.63% and a 3.50-3.75% target range - a two-basis-point spread that indicates no money-market dislocation whatsoever. The Fed's balance sheet stood at USD 6.738tn on 2026-07-29, having ended quantitative tightening on 2025-12-01 at roughly USD 6.57tn and grown by approximately USD 168bn since as the Fed resumed reserve-management purchases to match trend reserve demand. That is a marginally expansionary liquidity backdrop, not a contracting one, and it removes the mechanism by which a funding squeeze would force franc-funded positions to unwind. On the dollar smile, the USD sits firmly on the right-hand side - US exceptionalism with a hiking Fed - which is the quadrant in which the franc weakens against the dollar while potentially holding against other currencies, and the broad dollar index at 120.71 on 2026-07-24 is consistent with that, up 2.5% from its February low of 117.82 though still 0.8% below its year-ago level. The specific franc channel is now explicit: ING wrote on 2026-07-28 that reports of the SNB holding at zero until end-2027 point 'carry trade investors to increasingly fund out of Swiss francs rather than the yen' because franc funding is cheaper and avoids the risk of Bank of Japan intervention. Confidence is held to 60 rather than higher by a genuine and material data gap: no current numeric level for the 3M USD/CHF, EUR/USD or USD/JPY cross-currency basis is obtainable from free sources, which means the single most direct measure of USD funding stress cannot be verified this cycle. That gap is recorded explicitly rather than papered over.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices dollar funding as a non-issue and, on the evidence available, it is right - SOFR at 2bp over the effective funds rate is about as clean as a money market gets. The unpriced element is the reflexivity: because franc funding is now the marginal source of global carry leverage, any USD funding tightening would transmit to the franc faster and harder than it did in previous cycles, when the yen carried that role. We cannot measure the basis this cycle, so we hold the bearish stance at only 60 confidence and treat any widening in cross-currency basis as a first-order invalidation signal.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the USD liquidity backdrop is the second most consequential factor after policy rates, carrying a 0.12 strategic weight, and it stays franc-negative on the base case. The structural point is that the franc's new role in the global funding stack is a function of relative rates and relative intervention risk, both of which are stable over this horizon: the SNB is expected at zero until end-2027, while the BoJ is expected at 1.25% by year-end with the Japanese authorities demonstrably willing to intervene, which permanently taxes yen funding. As long as that configuration holds, franc-denominated borrowing is the cheapest leverage available anywhere, and the resulting flow is a persistent franc sale. The Fed's stance reinforces it: with QT concluded and the balance sheet growing modestly at USD 6.738tn, dollar liquidity is not the constraint it was in 2022-2023, and a Fed that is hiking into ample reserves produces the right-hand side of the dollar smile without the funding stress that historically accompanies tightening. The two identified strategic risks are specific. First, seasonality: cross-currency basis conventionally widens into year-end as bank balance sheets are constrained over the December turn, and the strategic window extends into that period; a franc-funded book meets its highest funding cost of the year exactly when liquidity is thinnest. Second, T-bill supply and reserve adequacy - if reserve balances fall toward the 'minimum comfortable level' the Fed would need to accelerate purchases, and the interim period would tighten money markets. Neither is a base case. Confidence is 58 rather than higher because the cross-currency basis, the one metric that would measure both risks directly, is unobtainable this cycle, so we are reasoning about a channel we cannot instrument.

tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the dossier is dominated by Policy & Rates at 0.24, Inflation & Growth at 0.18 and USD Liquidity at 0.11, which together carry 53% of the weight and all three point the same way for the franc. The reason they align is mechanical rather than narrative: the SNB policy rate is 0.00%, the lowest of the eleven benchmark currencies, and every single peer is either hiking or carries a hiking bias, so the average franc policy disadvantage of 269bp is widening rather than narrowing. That produces a net weighted score of -0.491 with six Bearish factors, four Neutral and none Bullish - a configuration in which the bearish result is generated by signal rather than by netting. The factor interactions reinforce rather than conflict: abundant dollar liquidity (SOFR at 3.65% just 2bp over effective funds, a Fed balance sheet growing again at USD 6.738tn) is what makes carry trades scalable, low volatility (EUR/CHF three-month implied at 3.77%) is what makes them leverageable, and a zero-rate SNB is what makes the franc the cheapest thing to sell - three conditions that are causally linked, not coincidental. The one genuinely conflicting input is the option skew, where risk reversals turn increasingly franc-call-bid as tenor extends, and the Neutral positioning read, which removes the squeeze risk that would normally cap a crowded funding trade. What is priced versus what we expect is the edge: forwards pay a 3.97% annualised franc appreciation cushion over one month, and we expect spot to move the other way, so the one-month expected return on a short-franc forward position is the 148-pip gap between the 0.80512 one-month outright and our 0.8200 expectation. The path of least resistance is a grind higher in USD/CHF through the 52-week high at 0.81938 toward 0.8250, because both primary pairs sit above all three major moving averages with bullish stacking, which means systematic flow reinforces the fundamental direction rather than opposing it. The dated catalysts inside the window are the Swiss July CPI and manufacturing PMI in the first week of August, the RBA on 2026-08-11, Norges Bank on 2026-08-13 and the Riksbank on 2026-08-20 - none of which can change the Swiss leg, which is itself the point: there is no scheduled mechanism by which the franc's disadvantage can improve before the SNB meets on 2026-09-24. Conviction drivers are that this is arithmetic rather than forecast (the rate gap exists whether or not our macro view is right), that positioning offers no squeeze fuel, and that the trend and vol regimes are both supportive. Actionability is high: USD/CHF three-month implied vol of 6.67% and a 2bp SOFR spread describe a liquid, functioning, low-cost market in which the view can be sized properly, and the carry pays roughly 24 pips a month while waiting.

g10_ranking.commentary: The franc ranks last of eleven tactically and we place it there without hedging. It has the lowest policy rate in the set at 0.00%, negative carry against all ten peers ranging from -100bp to -435bp, a central bank that has published a three-year forecast conditioned on doing nothing, and a real effective exchange rate at only the 40th percentile so no valuation floor. Every other currency in the set has at least one tactical support the franc lacks: NZD and NOK have published tightening paths, USD and GBP have hiking Fed and BoE pricing, SGD has a tightening MAS with 5.7% growth, JPY has 100bp more carry and a REER at the third percentile, and even CAD, with the weakest growth in the set at -0.05% year-on-year, still earns 225bp over the franc. The franc's structural advantages - a 9.77%-of-GDP surplus and an AAA sovereign - are real but do not transmit inside four weeks.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the framework redistributes materially: Policy & Rates holds at 0.24 but External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16, Guidance from 0.07 to 0.12, and USD Liquidity from 0.11 to 0.12, while Inflation & Growth falls from 0.18 to 0.10 and Risk Appetite halves to 0.05. That reweighting is why the strategic score of -0.240 is less than half the tactical -0.491: the same underlying facts produce a materially less bearish result once Switzerland's 9.77%-of-GDP current-account surplus and AAA sovereign are given the weight they deserve. Policy & Rates still dominates and still points down - the SNB's own conditional forecast conditions on 0.00% through 2028, Norges Bank has published a path above 4.5%, the Fed's dots centre on 3.6-4.1% and the average franc policy disadvantage widens from 269bp toward 295-305bp by January 2027 - and Guidance reinforces it, because a central bank that has pre-committed to inaction has removed the currency's optionality entirely. Those two factors interact: it is Guidance, not the rate level itself, that converted the franc from a cyclical low-yielder into the world's structural funding currency, and ING dated that conversion precisely to the 2026-07-28 reporting that SNB insiders see zero until end-2027. The conflicting inputs are External Balance and Fiscal, which contribute +0.124 between them and are the reason we bound the downside: a country running a near-10% external surplus, third only to Singapore and Norway, with a CHF 974bn net international investment position, 37.6% debt-to-GDP and a 0.475% ten-year yield does not sustain open-ended currency depreciation. What is priced versus what we expect is the clearest edge in the dossier: the six-month USD/CHF forward outright is 0.79113, embedding a 4.12% annualised franc appreciation, while we expect 0.8250 - a 339-pip gap and a total expected forward return of roughly 4.2%. Consensus is with us on EUR/CHF, where surveyed banks cluster at 0.92-0.95 and UBS is at 0.95 for end-2026, but decisively against us on USD/CHF, where UBS looks for stabilisation near 0.78. The path of least resistance is a slower version of the tactical grind, punctuated by the 2026-09-24 and 2026-12-10 SNB assessments, the 2026-09-03 SECO Q2 GDP release and the 2026-09-29 extension of pharmaceutical tariffs to all importers. Conviction drivers are the durability and specificity of the SNB's guidance and the fact that the carry is paid by the forward curve rather than requiring a spot forecast to be right. Actionability is good but requires structuring: we prefer forwards maturing before the December year-end basis turn, and we regard a small EUR/CHF put position at 3.77% three-month implied vol as inexpensive insurance against the one scenario that breaks the thesis.

strategic.path_expectation: The strategic path is a stepped grind punctuated by the central-bank calendar rather than a smooth trend. Phase one, August into early September, should extend the tactical move through the 52-week high at 0.81938 toward 0.8250 as the September central-bank cluster is priced. Phase two, around the 2026-09-24 SNB assessment and the 2026-09-29 full tariff extension, is where we expect the largest single-day volatility of the window and a genuine two-way risk: an SNB inflation-forecast revision in either direction reprices the franc curve, and the market's residual 12-25bp hawkish premium is the vehicle. Phase three, October to December, should be a slower drift toward 0.8250-0.8350 with the December year-end cross-currency basis turn the most likely source of a sharp, short-lived franc rally of 1-2% that we would fade rather than follow. We expect realised volatility to rise from the current 6.9% toward the 7.2% implied by one-year options, so pullbacks should be deeper and more frequent than in the tactical window - the 100-day moving average at 0.7952 is the level we expect to hold on the deepest of them. Pattern shape is a stair-step grind with event-driven gaps, not a trend channel.

risk_reward.downside_case_loss: USD/CHF 0.7800 is -278 pips or -3.44% of spot; net of the +167 pips of six-month carry the loss on a forward expression is -111 pips or -1.37%
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 3.1:1 (base case +339 pips including carry versus adverse case -111 pips including carry); 0.62:1 on spot alone, which is the honest statement that this is a carry trade rather than a directional one
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: Including carry the distribution is strongly skewed in our favour at roughly 3:1, but that ratio is manufactured entirely by the 4.12% annualised forward discount rather than by any expected spot move - on spot alone the trade is unfavourable at 0.62:1. That is the single most important disclosure in this dossier: the strategic franc short is a carry harvest with a bounded expected spot gain and an unbounded tail loss, and it must be sized as such. The Fiscal and External Balance factors are what bound the downside at USD/CHF 0.8600; nothing bounds the upside for the franc except the SNB's willingness to intervene, and the January 2015 precedent establishes that SNB behaviour is not a reliable stop.

consensus_divergence.consensus_view: The surveyed bank consensus is mildly bearish on the franc against the euro. On EUR/CHF the majority of banks in the June 2026 survey see 0.92-0.95 through 2027, with BofA, Credit Agricole, SEB, Scotiabank, UBS and Citi clustered at 0.93-0.95 over twelve to twenty-four months and a more cautious camp - Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Westpac and Danske - at 0.90-0.91. That survey is dated 2026-06-09, 53 days before the valuation date, so it pre-dates the July FOMC, the 2026-07-31 tariff onset and the funding-currency reassignment - flagged. On USD/CHF, NO dated bank-consensus grid at 3M/6M/12M horizons could be sourced from free data this cycle; a 0.78 UBS stabilisation figure carried in an earlier draft was WITHDRAWN on adversarial verification because the cited survey does not mention USD/CHF at all. The USD/CHF consensus is therefore recorded as a documented gap. On policy, consensus is near-unanimous: a Reuters poll reportedly found 28 of 29 forecasters expecting no SNB change through 2026, and Commerzbank and ING both see zero until end-2027.
consensus_divergence.our_view: We expect USD/CHF at 0.8200 in one month, 0.8230 in three and 0.8250 in six, and EUR/CHF at 0.9400, 0.9430 and 0.9450 respectively. That places us at the weak-franc end of the EUR/CHF consensus range but broadly within it, and decisively outside the consensus on USD/CHF, where we look for the franc to weaken by 1.8% over six months against a consensus expecting it to strengthen by roughly 3.5%. We agree with consensus on the SNB - zero through the horizon - but we draw the opposite currency conclusion from it, because a pre-committed central bank removes the franc's optionality rather than protecting it.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Against the market, which is the only verifiable benchmark available this cycle: 148 pips (1.84%) at one month, 233 pips (2.92%) at three months and 339 pips (4.28%) at six months on USD/CHF versus the forward outrights of 0.80512, 0.79968 and 0.79113. Against the sell side, we sit roughly 100-150 pips (1.1-1.6%) above the centre of gravity of the EUR/CHF bank survey range at the six-month horizon. The previously stated 450-pip USD/CHF divergence was withdrawn on verification because its 0.78 consensus anchor could not be sourced.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: We differ on USD/CHF because consensus is underweighting four things. First, the market still carries 12-25bp of hawkish premium in the CHF front end against an SNB whose own conditional inflation forecast is constructed on a flat 0.00% through 2028 - that premium should decay, and the surveyed EUR/CHF forecasts implicitly assume it does not. Second, consensus has not fully absorbed the structural reassignment of the franc from haven to funding currency, which ING dated precisely to the 2026-07-28 reporting that SNB insiders see zero until end-2027; funding-currency status is a persistent flow, not a sentiment. Third, the regime has changed underneath the forecasts - the ECB hiked on 2026-06-11, the BoJ on 2026-06-16, the RBNZ on 2026-07-08 and the Fed has three hawkish dissenters, so the 2024-2025 easing cycle in which USD/CHF fell no longer describes the world. Fourth, consensus treats the Swiss external surplus as a currency support without acknowledging that a USD 200bn Swiss corporate investment pledge into the United States and a 15% pharmaceutical tariff both work against it. We are also explicit about what we do not claim: the gold drawdown of 17.94% over six months and the flat CHF-gold correlation are evidence for our view but they are also the fastest thing that could reverse.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A six-month short-CHF/long-USD forward position returns approximately +4.20%, comprising +2.13% of spot and +2.07% of carry, against a 0.79113 six-month outright. Because no verifiable USD/CHF consensus anchor exists this cycle, the payoff is stated against the forward curve rather than against a sell-side target - which is the more conservative and the more tradeable of the two benchmarks.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the franc-upside scenario is right and USD/CHF converges toward 0.78, the spot loss of 278 pips is offset to -111 pips by carry - a tolerable outcome. The real risk is not consensus being right but the tail being realised: the franc's adverse distribution has no natural stop, the January 2015 floor removal produced a roughly 30% intraday move with no prior guidance, and the same low volatility that makes this trade attractive is what makes it crowded. A 3-4% franc rally in a fortnight, which is the historical template for a funding-currency unwind, would wipe out more than eighteen months of carry.

cleanest_bearish_expression.rationale: USD/CHF combines the widest policy differential among the liquid franc crosses at 363bp with the strongest structural alignment - spot at 0.80779 sits above the 100-day at 0.7952 and the 200-day at 0.7927, all stacked bullishly - and the most favourable catalyst calendar, with the FOMC on 2026-09-16 the single largest scheduled event affecting the pair. ING explicitly identified USD/CHF as the market's chosen vehicle for expressing hawkish Fed views. Three-month implied volatility of 6.67% keeps the expression liquid and reasonably priced, twenty-day realised volatility of 6.9% running above implied favours spot or forward over options, and the three-month forward outright of 0.79968 pays 81 pips of carry over the holding period.

cleanest_bullish_expression.rationale: If the franc-bullish invalidation scenario materialises, EUR/CHF is the cleanest expression because it strips out the dollar entirely and isolates Swiss versus European fundamentals plus SNB policy - which is precisely the pair the SNB itself cares most about. At 3.43% one-month and 3.77% three-month implied volatility it is the cheapest optionality in the franc complex in absolute terms, so a franc-strength view can be owned as convexity rather than carried as spot against a 225bp negative differential. The offset to be explicit about is that the skew is already against the buyer: 25-delta risk reversals are negative at every tenor from -0.29 at one month to -0.74 at one year, so franc calls are the bid side and the hedge is cheap in vol terms but not in skew terms.

relative_value_pairs.thesis: The purest relative-value expression in the franc complex. The carry gap is only 225bp, the second smallest among the high-yielding bloc, and CAD/CHF proxy volatility of 6.71% is the second lowest, so the vol-adjusted cost of being long francs here is -0.34 versus -0.54 against the dollar. On fundamentals Canada is the weakest economy in the set at -0.05% GDP year-on-year with the Bank of Canada frozen at 2.25% through Q1 2027 on its own Market Participants Survey, while CAD leveraged-fund positioning at -98,377 contracts sits at the 4th percentile of the cached window - an extreme short with squeeze risk that could work either way but is priced as one-sided.

The maximum-carry franc short at 435bp annualised, the widest differential in the set. The caveat is valuation: the Australian REER at 115.92 sits at the 97th percentile of the cached window and 6.4% above its mean, the most stretched real exchange rate of the eleven, and AUD has already appreciated 9.47% against the dollar over twelve months, so the carry is being harvested against a currency with no valuation runway. Carry-max, valuation-capped - suitable as a small carry sleeve rather than the core expression.

The relative safe-haven trade, and the cheapest way to be long francs anywhere: the carry cost is only 100bp against a proxy volatility of 8.49%, a ratio of -0.12 versus -0.54 against the dollar. The thesis is that the market has over-rotated in designating the franc as the funding currency of choice over the yen, when the BoJ is hiking toward 1.25% and the Japanese REER at 65.30 sits at the 3rd percentile - the most undervalued currency in the set. This is a hedge against our own thesis rather than an expression of it, and it is where a franc bull should express the view.

cross_horizon_consistency.summary: Both horizons are Bearish on the franc, but the intensity decays sharply with time: tactical conviction 4 on a net score of -0.4915 versus strategic conviction 3 on -0.2401, with overall confidence falling from 64 to 61.
cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: The stances agree but the magnitudes do not, and the reason is entirely in the weight schedule rather than in any change of view. External Balance carries 0.06 tactically and 0.16 strategically, and Fiscal & Sovereign 0.04 versus 0.07 - so the two factors on which Switzerland is structurally strongest are nearly tripled in weight as the horizon extends, contributing +0.124 strategically against essentially nothing tactically. Simultaneously Inflation & Growth is cut from 0.18 to 0.10 and Risk Appetite from 0.10 to 0.05, removing weight from two factors on which Switzerland is cyclically weak. Three individual factors also change stance across the split - Inflation & Growth from Bearish to Neutral, External Balance from Neutral to Bullish, and Fiscal from Neutral to Bullish - each for a mechanistic reason set out in its horizon-split explanation.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The thesis weakens progressively rather than at a single point, but the identifiable inflection is the 2026-09-24 SNB monetary policy assessment. Before it, no scheduled event can change the Swiss leg of the differential, so the tactical thesis runs unopposed. At it, the SNB revises its conditional inflation forecast for the first time since the energy shock re-intensified, and that revision is the mechanism by which the residual 12-25bp of hawkish front-end premium either decays - extending the thesis - or is validated, which would mark the strategic turn.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: Swiss headline CPI sustaining above 1.0% year-on-year with the SFSO core measure above 0.6%, which would force a genuine repricing of the 2027 SNB path and flip Factor 2 from Neutral to Bullish and Factor 6 from Bearish to Neutral - a swing of roughly +0.14 on the strategic score, taking it to approximately -0.10 and conviction 1. The alternative transition catalyst is exogenous: a VIX close above 26 for three sessions flipping Factor 3.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Carry the position with a tactical horizon and a strategic stop rather than the reverse: the highest-quality part of the expected return is concentrated in the next four to six weeks, before the 2026-09-24 SNB assessment, while the six-month expected return is dominated by carry rather than spot at a 0.62:1 spot-only risk-reward. Practically that argues for forwards maturing before the December year-end basis turn, with position size reduced after the September SNB assessment unless the conviction ladder's increase conditions have been met.

forward_vs_spot.interpretation: The forward curve pays a holder of dollars against francs approximately 4% annualised, which is simply the interest differential expressed as price and contains no view. Our expected spot path moves against the forward at every tenor, so the two sources of return compound rather than offset: at six months the expected +2.13% of spot movement is added to the +2.07% already embedded in the forward points for a total of roughly +4.2%. The corresponding statement for a franc bull is stark - a long-franc position must deliver better than 0.33% of appreciation per month against the dollar just to match the forward, and EUR/CHF must fall below 0.92570 within three months for a long-franc euro-cross position to break even. Forward points are mid-market derived from published bid/ask; the outrights are our own calculation from cached spot, as neither source publishes outright forward rates.

seasonality.pattern: Two seasonal considerations fall inside the horizons and both are market-structure effects rather than documented directional patterns, and are presented as such. First, August European liquidity thins materially, which does not create direction but amplifies whatever direction emerges - a franc-funded carry book carries its largest gap risk in the weeks when depth is lowest. Second, cross-currency basis conventionally widens into the December year-end turn as bank balance sheets are constrained, which raises the cost of franc-funded positions precisely when liquidity is thinnest. We deliberately do not assert a directional Swiss seasonal pattern, because none is documented for the franc in the way March and September repatriation flows are documented for the yen.
seasonality.relevance_window: August thin-liquidity risk applies to the entire tactical window (2026-08 to 2026-09); the December year-end basis turn falls in the final month of the strategic window (2026-12)
seasonality.historical_magnitude: Not quantified from a sourced series this cycle - recorded as an observation rather than a measured effect. The general August funding-currency template of a 3-4% move in a fortnight is referenced from the behaviour of carry unwinds rather than from a Swiss-specific statistical study.
seasonality.current_alignment: Both effects run against the position rather than with it. This is the specific reason the strategic section recommends forwards maturing before the December turn and reduced sizing after the 2026-09-24 SNB assessment, rather than a single six-month holding period.

EUR/CHF IS DERIVED, NOT OBSERVED. The cache carries USD/CHF and EUR/USD but not EUR/CHF. EUR/CHF 0.9317 is calculated as 1.15335 x 0.80779. The SNB's own 2026-07-31 fixing was EUR/CHF 0.9291 and USD/CHF 0.8064 - a 26-pip and 14-pip difference respectively attributable to different fixing times. PPP TABLE IS A REER-DIFFERENTIAL PROXY, NOT AN ABSOLUTE PPP ESTIMATE. No sourced absolute PPP dataset was available this cycle. The ppp_table deviations are computed as (Switzerland BIS real broad REER / peer BIS real broad REER - 1) x 100 using June 2026 values on the common index base. Because BIS REER indices measure change from a common base rather than absolute price-level parity, these figures express relative real appreciation since that base, not distance from an absolute fair value. Implied fair values are back-solved from spot on the same basis. Treat as an ordinal ranking of relative richness rather than as point estimates.

IV PERCENTILE IS ESTIMATED, NOT OBSERVED. iv_percentile_1y of 45 for USD/CHF is inferred from the cached realised-volatility distribution (1M 6.9%, 3M 5.9%, 12M 6.2%) against current 1M implied of 6.52%. No free source publishes a one-year implied-volatility distribution for USD/CHF or EUR/CHF. This is a documented gap and the figure should not be relied upon as a true percentile.

CROSS-CURRENCY BASIS IS UNAVAILABLE. No current numeric level for the 3M USD/CHF, 3M EUR/USD or 3M USD/JPY cross-currency basis could be sourced from free web data as of the valuation date. Factor 10 is therefore assessed without its primary instrument and its confidence is capped at 60 tactical and 58 strategic for that reason. Any basis widening should be treated as a first-order invalidation signal that this dossier cannot currently measure.

CARRY-TO-VOL DENOMINATORS ARE MIXED. Carry-to-volatility ratios use observed 3M ATM implied volatility where available (USD/CHF 6.67%, EUR/CHF 3.77%, Saxo snapshot 2026-07-31 07:00 GMT). For crosses without an observed implied vol (AUD/CHF, GBP/CHF, CHF/JPY, CAD/CHF, CHF/SGD) the denominator is a proxy computed as the square root of the sum of the squared cached 3M realised volatilities of the peer's USD pair and USD/CHF, i.e. assuming zero correlation. This is deliberately conservative and overstates the proxy volatility, so the vol-adjusted carry costs for those crosses are understated in magnitude.

FORWARD OUTRIGHTS ARE CALCULATED AND DO NOT RECONCILE TO THE POLICY GAP ALONE. Investing.com publishes forward points but not outright forward rates. Outrights (USD/CHF 1M 0.80512, 3M 0.79968, 6M 0.79113) are computed as cached spot 0.80779 less mid forward points. An earlier draft claimed the outrights 'sanity-check against the observed policy and money-market differentials'; that claim was withdrawn on adversarial verification. STANCE-TO-SCORE MAPPING AND CONVICTION LADDER. Bullish = +1, Neutral = 0, Bearish = -1; confidence-adjusted score = stance score x confidence / 100; weighted contribution = confidence-adjusted score x horizon weight. Conviction is mapped from the absolute net score as: below 0.10 = 1, 0.10-0.20 = 2, 0.20-0.35 = 3, 0.35-0.55 = 4, above 0.55 = 5. Overall confidence is the weight-weighted average of the ten factor confidences at that horizon. Both weight columns sum to exactly 1.00 and the arithmetic in both weighted-score tables reconciles to the stated net scores.
